extracted.intended_audience: public company registrants (issuers), GHG emissions attestation providers (accountant and non-accountant), auditors, audit committees, and securities/ compliance counsel
extracted.subtask_description: Rules and guidance governing GHG emissions attestation engagements and reports under the SEC's Item 1506, including provider independence, acceptable attestation standards, report form/content, assurance levels, phase-in timing, and related procedural exhibit/consent rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Independence requirement for GHG emissions attestation providers
rubrics_metrics.description: The final rules require that a GHG emissions attestation provider be independent in accordance with Item 1506; the Commission will consider factors such as whether the provider would be attesting to its own work or whether a mutual interest exists between the provider and the registrant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commenters raised concerns that an independence requirement could limit providers and increase costs; the Commission relied on a multi-year phased compliance period to mitigate those effects. The Commission rejected alternatives (e.g., merely disclosing fees) because disclosure alone would not prevent non-independent providers from performing assurance. The independence requirement is intended to prevent conflicts of interest (for example, a third-party who helped prepare emissions data likely cannot be independent). The independence analysis will consider affiliates and the attestation/professional engagement period (modeled on Rule 2-01).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of affiliate and attestation/professional engagement period
rubrics_metrics.description: The final rules adopt the proposed definition of 'affiliate' and a broad definition of 'attestation and professional engagement period' modeled on Rule 2-01.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These definitions are used in assessing whether an attestation provider meets independence requirements and in identifying potential conflicts of interest under Item 1506.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attestation standards must be developed using due process
rubrics_metrics.description: The attestation report must be provided pursuant to standards that are established by a body or group that has followed due process procedures, including broad distribution of the framework for public comment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Commission views due process as ensuring the standards are the result of a transparent, public, and reasoned process and helpful to protect investors. Examples cited as meeting this requirement include PCAOB, AICPA, and IAASB standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attestation standards must be publicly available or widely used
rubrics_metrics.description: Final rules require the attestation report be provided pursuant to standards that, in addition to being developed using due process, are either (i) publicly available at no cost, or (ii) widely used for GHG emissions assurance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Commission modified the proposal (which had required standards to be publicly available at no cost) to allow widely used standards (e.g., ISO 14064-3) even if not free, reasoning that widely used standards provide investors and market participants significant experience and reduce compliance costs. PCAOB/AICPA/IAASB are publicly available and meet due process; ISO standards were found to align with due process though they are not free.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form and content of the attestation report must follow the attestation standard(s) used
rubrics_metrics.description: The form and content of the GHG emissions attestation report must follow the requirements set forth by the attestation standard or standards used by the attestation provider.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unlike the proposal, the final rules do not prescribe minimum report requirements; the Commission expects suitable attestation standards will generally include the common elements of assurance reports. If a particular standard does not include elements commonly included in assurance reports, the attestation provider should consider including such information to facilitate investors' understanding of the nature and scope of the engagement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposed minimum attestation report components (not adopted)
rubrics_metrics.description: The proposal had included minimum attestation engagement and report requirements (primarily derived from AICPA SSAE No. 18 and similar to PCAOB AT-101 and IAASB ISAE 3410) to standardize reports.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many commenters agreed these were common elements of current assurance reports. The Commission concluded that prescribing minimum components would be marginal/redundant because attestation standards generally include these elements, and therefore did not carry them forward into the final rules. Nonetheless, the elements inform expectations about typical report content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assurance level distinctions and Section 11 treatment
rubrics_metrics.description: The Commission treats limited assurance and reasonable assurance differently: reports covering Scope 1 and/or Scope 2 emissions at the limited assurance level are not considered part of the registration statement prepared or certified by an expert under sections 7 and 11 of the Securities Act; reasonable assurance engagements remain subject to section 11 liability and consent requirements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The limited-assurance exception is intended to encourage providers to perform limited assurance by removing potential Section 11 liability that could deter providers or increase costs. The exception is limited to limited assurance; if providers perform substantially expanded procedures akin to reasonable assurance, the exemption would not apply.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exhibit/consent filing and attestation provider awareness letter
rubrics_metrics.description: A GHG emissions attestation provider that performed a limited-assurance engagement is not required to submit a consent under Section 7, but registrants must file as an exhibit a letter from the attestation provider acknowledging awareness of the use in certain registration statements of any of its reports not subject to the consent requirement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This amendment to Item 601 (and Form 20-F Instructions) preserves awareness by providers when their reports are used in registration statements and substitutes an awareness/acknowledgment exhibit for the Section 7 consent where the limited-assurance exception applies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identification of criteria against which subject matter is measured
rubrics_metrics.description: The attestation report should identify the criteria against which the subject matter (e.g., Scope 1 and Scope 2 emissions) was measured or evaluated; referencing Item 1504 or the registrant's chosen public standard (e.g., GHG Protocol) can meet the 'suitable criteria' requirement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commenters largely agreed that the GHG Protocol would qualify as suitable criteria if required or permitted by the Commission, though some commenters expressed that reporting standards are not yet fully developed for reliable GHG measurement. The attestation report should make clear what criteria/methodology were used so investors can evaluate the report.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quality control and management system expectations for attestation providers
rubrics_metrics.description: The Commission determined not to impose additional minimum quality control requirements in the final rules, relying on existing professional quality control regimes where applicable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accountants are already required to comply with PCAOB, AICPA, or IAASB quality control and management standards when providing audit and attest services; IAASB standards impose similar requirements on non-accountants, and many experienced non-accountant providers are accredited and subject to QC requirements. The Commission expects that attestation standards that meet the final rules will provide guidance on quality control for assurance providers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audit committee role and auditor-performed attestations
rubrics_metrics.description: The final rules do not require audit committee pre-approval of GHG emissions attestation services, but a registrant may use its financial statement auditor to perform the GHG attestation engagement provided the provider meets the final rules' requirements; where existing pre-approval requirements apply, the auditor must comply with them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even where pre-approval is not required, the Commission encourages audit committees to consider an appropriate level of involvement in selection and retention of attestation providers for climate-related disclosures. If the registrant's auditor is engaged, applicable pre-approval rules for auditor services remain in effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Phased-in coverage of historical periods for attestation reports
rubrics_metrics.description: The attestation requirement applies prospectively with historical-period disclosure phasing in over time: in the first year an AF or LAF must provide an attestation report it is required only to cover Scope 1 and/or Scope 2 emissions for its most recently completed fiscal year; each subsequent fiscal year's annual report must include an attestation report for an additional fiscal year until the entire period covered by the registrant's GHG disclosures is attested.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This phased approach addresses commenters' requests for clarity and mitigates burdens by not requiring immediate attestation of multiple historical years in year one of applicability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of voluntary Scope 3 limited-assurance engagements
rubrics_metrics.description: A report covering Scope 3 emissions at a limited assurance level shall not be considered part of the registration statement prepared or certified by an expert under sections 7 and 11, in the event a registrant voluntarily discloses Scope 3 emissions and obtains limited assurance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Including Scope 3 within the limited-assurance exception is intended to encourage voluntary assurance over Scope 3 disclosures; no registrants are required to disclose or obtain attestation for Scope 3 under the final rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding self-attestation and resulting duplicative fees
rubrics_metrics.description: An expert or third-party that assisted a registrant in calculating or preparing its GHG emissions data likely cannot meet the independence requirements (because attesting to one's own work or having a mutual interest undermines independence).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Commission declined to modify the independence requirement to allow such preparers to serve as attestation providers. As a result, registrants that hire third parties to prepare emissions data may need to pay both the preparer and an independent attestation provider. The phased-in compliance period and SRC/EGC exemptions are intended to reduce the likelihood this causes undue burden for newly public companies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Flexible approach to acceptable attestation standards (no single mandated standard)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Commission favors a flexible approach to acceptable attestation standards rather than prescribing a single required standard or providing a finite list of acceptable standards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although PCAOB, AICPA, IAASB, and ISO standards are explicitly noted as meeting the due process/widely-used criteria, the Commission recognizes other standards may be suitable now or in the future. Commenters suggested alternative approaches (e.g., a list or a process to assess sufficiency); the Commission chose flexibility to allow multiple suitable standards and future development.
